Courts also convicted 25 FARDC soldiers, 10 police officers, seven intelligence agents, and 62 armed-group members for rights-related crimes.","locator":"Paragraphs 25-29, PDF pp. 5-6","provisional_id":"WEB-3B-001","canonical_fact_key":"https://documents.un.org/doc/undoc/gen/n22/376/90/pdf/n2237690.pdf?OpenElement=|paras 25-29|March-April violations, state killings, and convictions","disposition":"final_evidence","chapter_ids":["3B"],"methodology_ids":["3B.1","3B.2","3B.4","3B.6","3B.10"],"source_type":"intergovernmental monitoring report","source_confidence":"high","source_confidence_reason":"Contemporaneous UN monitoring with numerical attribution, while allegations and documented cases are not national prevalence estimates.","final_evidence_use":"final_evidence","period_fit":"Direct March-April 2022 evidence.","ruler_attribution":"National forces and justice institutions operated under Tshisekedi, but the report does not establish his knowledge of individual abuses or prosecutions.","contrary_evidence":["The same record documents both serious FARDC abuse and criminal convictions of security personnel.","Armed groups allegedly caused a majority of documented violations."],"lenses":["3B.1","3B.2","3B.4","3B.6","3B.10"]}

SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON: {"title":"Le Président Félix Tshisekedi a reçu les représentants des communautés congolaises tutsi et hutu pour parler de la cohésion nationale","publisher":"Présidence de la République démocratique du Congo","publication_date":"2022-11-11","url":"https://presidence.cd/actualite-detail/actualite/le_president_felix_tshisekedi_a_recu_les_representants_des_communautes_congolaises_tutsi_et_hutu_pour_parler_de_la_cohesion_nationale","claim":"Tshisekedi met Congolese Tutsi and Hutu representatives and publicly affirmed that all Congolese should live without ethnic discrimination, while opposing ethnic stigmatization and physical profiling.","locator":"Article paragraphs corresponding to displayed lines 67-75, especially lines 70-75","provisional_id":"WEB-3B-002","canonical_fact_key":"https://presidence.cd/actualite-detail/actualite/le_president_felix_tshisekedi_a_recu_les_representants_des_communautes_congolaises_tutsi_et_hutu_pour_parler_de_la_cohesion_nationale|paras 1-5|presidential anti-discrimination message","disposition":"final_evidence","chapter_ids":["3B"],"methodology_ids":["3B.3","3B.7","3B.9"],"source_type":"official presidential record","source_confidence":"medium","source_confidence_reason":"Strong evidence of the president’s own stated position but not independent evidence of implementation or protection outcomes.","final_evidence_use":"final_evidence","period_fit":"Direct November 2022 presidential action and statement.","ruler_attribution":"Direct personal attribution to Tshisekedi.","contrary_evidence":["UN reporting documented escalating hate speech against Kinyarwanda speakers during the same conflict.","The official account does not establish whether perpetrators were punished or threatened communities became safer."],"lenses":["3B.3","3B.7","3B.9"]}

SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON: {"title":"DRC police detain, beat 3 journalists covering protest","publisher":"Committee to Protect Journalists","publication_date":"2022-09-02","url":"https://cpj.org/2022/09/drc-police-detain-beat-3-journalists-covering-protest/","claim":"Police arrested three journalists covering an opposition protest in Kinshasa; one reported being punched and injured, while all were subsequently released unconditionally, two on the provincial police commissioner’s order.","locator":"Article paragraphs displayed at lines 515-526","provisional_id":"WEB-3B-003","canonical_fact_key":"https://cpj.org/2022/09/drc-police-detain-beat-3-journalists-covering-protest/|paras 1-8|three journalists arrested and one beaten at August protest","disposition":"final_evidence","chapter_ids":["3B"],"methodology_ids":["3B.2","3B.8"],"source_type":"press-freedom organization incident investigation","source_confidence":"medium-high","source_confidence_reason":"Named victims, dates, injury, interviews, and release details; accountability after release was not demonstrated.","final_evidence_use":"final_evidence","period_fit":"Direct August-September 2022 incident.","ruler_attribution":"Police-chain responsibility is relevant to the national administration, but no evidence connects Tshisekedi personally to the arrests.","contrary_evidence":["The journalists were released quickly and unconditionally.","The source called for investigation but did not document completed discipline or prosecution."],"lenses":["3B.2","3B.8"]}

SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON: {"title":"En RD Congo, un premier pas vers la justice dans l’affaire Chebeya","publisher":"Human Rights Watch","publication_date":"2022-05-12","url":"https://www.hrw.org/fr/news/2022/05/12/en-rd-congo-un-premier-pas-vers-la-justice-dans-laffaire-chebeya","claim":"The High Military Court upheld convictions of two senior police officers for the 2010 murders of Floribert Chebeya and Fidèle Bazana, but the former police chief alleged to have ordered the murders had still not been investigated.","locator":"Paragraphs displayed at lines 654-662","provisional_id":"WEB-3B-004","canonical_fact_key":"https://www.hrw.org/fr/news/2022/05/12/en-rd-congo-un-premier-pas-vers-la-justice-dans-laffaire-chebeya|paras 1-6|appeal convictions with principal alleged organizer uninvestigated","disposition":"final_evidence","chapter_ids":["3B"],"methodology_ids":["3B.2","3B.4"],"source_type":"human-rights case analysis","source_confidence":"high","source_confidence_reason":"Specific appellate outcome and sentences, with a clearly identified unresolved accountability limitation.","final_evidence_use":"final_evidence","period_fit":"The appellate judgment occurred in May 2022, although the murders were inherited from 2010.","ruler_attribution":"The appeal proceeded under Tshisekedi; the case was inherited and civil-society advocacy was a major driver.","contrary_evidence":["Two police officers were held accountable.","The alleged senior organizer remained outside an effective investigation, limiting evidence of complete remedy."],"lenses":["3B.2","3B.4"]}

SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON: {"title":"Amnesty International Report 2022/23: Democratic Republic of the Congo","publisher":"Amnesty International","publication_date":"2023-03-27","url":"https://www.amnesty.be/infos/rapports-annuels/rapport-annuel-2022/rapport-annuel-2022-afrique/article/republique-democratique-congo-rapport-annuel-2022","claim":"Authorities continued arbitrary detention and protest suppression under the state of siege; police violently suppressed a peaceful doctors’ demonstration in Kinshasa, while a North Kivu appellate court separately overturned the military-court convictions of detained LUCHA activists.","locator":"Sections on impunity and freedoms, displayed lines 134-148","provisional_id":"WEB-3B-005","canonical_fact_key":"https://www.amnesty.be/infos/rapports-annuels/rapport-annuel-2022/rapport-annuel-2022-afrique/article/republique-democratique-congo-rapport-annuel-2022|lines 134-148|protest repression and successful LUCHA appeal","disposition":"final_evidence","chapter_ids":["3B"],"methodology_ids":["3B.4","3B.5","3B.8","3B.9"],"source_type":"annual human-rights review","source_confidence":"high","source_confidence_reason":"Multiple specific incidents and judicial outcomes; the review also distinguishes violent anti-UN protests from the peaceful doctors’ march.","final_evidence_use":"final_evidence","period_fit":"Direct 2022 events and outcomes.","ruler_attribution":"Emergency arrangements and national security forces fall within Tshisekedi’s formal authority, but local decisions are not necessarily personal orders.","contrary_evidence":["The appellate reversal and activists’ release show a functioning corrective mechanism in one case.","Amnesty found no effective remedy following the doctors’ protest crackdown."],"lenses":["3B.4","3B.5","3B.8","3B.9"]}

SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON: {"title":"2022 Country Report on Human Rights Practices: Democratic Republic of the Congo","publisher":"United States Department of State","publication_date":"2023-03-20","url":"https://www.ecoi.net/en/document/2089109.html","claim":"The government expanded police and military training and action plans addressing child protection and sexual violence, but UN monitoring attributed 54 conflict-related sexual-violence survivors in January-June to FARDC personnel and found state agents responsible for nearly 18 percent of 239 documented cases.","locator":"Executive/security-force measures at lines 78-79; conflict-related sexual violence and action plans at lines 157-164","provisional_id":"WEB-3B-006","canonical_fact_key":"https://www.ecoi.net/en/document/2089109.html|sections 1g and children|protection training alongside state-agent sexual violence","disposition":"final_evidence","chapter_ids":["3B"],"methodology_ids":["3B.2","3B.4","3B.7"],"source_type":"government human-rights country report synthesizing UN and NGO evidence","source_confidence":"medium-high","source_confidence_reason":"Detailed and source-attributed synthesis; partly dependent on UN reporting and should not be treated as an independent duplicate of the underlying UN observations.","final_evidence_use":"final_evidence","period_fit":"Direct January-June 2022 monitoring and 2022 institutional actions.","ruler_attribution":"National action plans and training are administration-level measures; individual sexual-violence incidents are not personally attributed to Tshisekedi.","contrary_evidence":["Training and action plans indicate preventive effort.","Continued FARDC abuse shows that operational protection remained incomplete."],"lenses":["3B.2","3B.4","3B.7"]}

SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON: {"title":"2022 Country Report on Human Rights Practices: Democratic Republic of the Congo","publisher":"United States Department of State","publication_date":"2023-03-20","url":"https://www.ecoi.net/en/document/2089109.html","claim":"UNJHRO recorded 1,505 civilians killed in conflict-affected provinces in the first half of 2022, including 123 children; armed groups caused most killings, while FARDC and police also contributed, and conflict operations caused major displacement despite government-MONUSCO protection cooperation.","locator":"Conflict-abuse section, lines 144-166, especially 150-166","provisional_id":"WEB-3B-007","canonical_fact_key":"https://www.ecoi.net/en/document/2089109.html|section 1g lines 144-166|civilian deaths displacement and protection cooperation","disposition":"final_evidence","chapter_ids":["3B"],"methodology_ids":["3B.1","3B.6","3B.7","3B.9","3B.10"],"source_type":"government human-rights country report synthesizing UN and NGO evidence","source_confidence":"medium-high","source_confidence_reason":"Quantified UNJHRO-derived outcomes and identified actor mix; conflict-zone access and double-counting risks constrain national inference.","final_evidence_use":"final_evidence","period_fit":"Direct first-half 2022 evidence.","ruler_attribution":"Tshisekedi had authority over FARDC direction and protection cooperation, but armed groups caused most recorded killings and inherited conflict severely constrained control.","contrary_evidence":["Government-MONUSCO patrols and humanitarian coordination sought to protect displaced people.","The record does not demonstrate that these measures outweighed worsening insecurity or state-agent abuse."],"lenses":["3B.1","3B.6","3B.7","3B.9","3B.10"]}

SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON: {"title":"DRC: One year on, ‘State of Siege’ used as a tool to crush dissent","publisher":"Amnesty International","publication_date":"2022-05-10","url":"https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2022/05/drc-one-year-on-state-of-siege/","claim":"Under the state of siege, security forces killed two peaceful activists and military authorities arbitrarily detained critics; civilian deaths in North Kivu and Ituri increased from 559 in June 2020-March 2021 to at least 1,261 in June 2021-March 2022, while military-court jurisdiction over civilians worsened pretrial detention.","locator":"Opening summary and sections displayed at lines 64-104, especially 75-91","provisional_id":"WEB-3B-008","canonical_fact_key":"https://www.amnesty.org/en/latest/news/2022/05/drc-one-year-on-state-of-siege/|lines 64-104|state of siege repression and increased civilian deaths","disposition":"final_evidence","chapter_ids":["3B"],"methodology_ids":["3B.1","3B.4","3B.5","3B.6","3B.8","3B.10"],"source_type":"human-rights thematic investigation","source_confidence":"high","source_confidence_reason":"Specific cases and comparative UN death figures; the before/after comparison does not by itself prove that emergency rule caused the conflict increase.","final_evidence_use":"final_evidence","period_fit":"Covers the state of siege through March-May 2022.","ruler_attribution":"Amnesty directly attributes the military-court policy to Tshisekedi; individual abuses remain command/system-level rather than proven personal orders.","contrary_evidence":["The emergency was introduced with the stated purpose of protecting civilians amid inherited armed conflict.","Temporal deterioration does not isolate policy causation from armed-group escalation."],"lenses":["3B.1","3B.4","3B.5","3B.6","3B.8","3B.10"]}

SOURCE_CLAIM_JSON: {"title":"Response to escalation by DRC","publisher":"Government of Rwanda","publication_date":"2022-10-30","url":"https://www.gov.rw/blog-detail/response-to-escalation-by-drc","claim":"Rwanda alleged that Congolese officials used anti-Rwanda rhetoric and that officials and members of the public engaged in hate speech and harassment against Rwandans and Kinyarwanda-speaking Congolese.","locator":"Press release lines 21-32, especially lines 26-30","provisional_id":"WEB-3B-010","canonical_fact_key":"https://www.gov.rw/blog-detail/response-to-escalation-by-drc|lines 21-32|Rwandan allegation of official hate speech and scapegoating","disposition":"context","chapter_ids":["3B"],"methodology_ids":["3B.3","3B.7","3B.9"],"source_type":"adverse foreign-government statement","source_confidence":"low-medium","source_confidence_reason":"Direct evidence of Rwanda’s contemporary allegation, but Rwanda was an interested conflict party and the statement does not identify precise speakers or independently verify incidents.","final_evidence_use":"context","period_fit":"Direct October 2022 contrary interpretation.","ruler_attribution":"Criticism concerns Tshisekedi’s government generally, not a verified personal incitement by Tshisekedi.","contrary_evidence":["Tshisekedi later personally affirmed protection and nondiscrimination for Congolese Tutsi and Hutu communities.","UN reporting independently confirmed escalating anti-Kinyarwanda hate speech, but not personal incitement by Tshisekedi in the material inspected."],"lenses":["3B.3","3B.7","3B.9"]}

Research-accounting summary:

- Plausible documents inspected during discovery: approximately 36.
- Underlying pages/reports opened or directly attempted: 24.
- Successfully opened: 18.
- Accepted new units: 10 — nine `final_evidence`, one `context`.
- Reused and directly reverified records: 6 — E006, E007, E008, E011, E027, E042.
- Rejected after inspection: 12, mainly wrong-year reports, duplicative summaries, secondary restatements, or claims lacking precise attribution.
- Access-blocked or fetch-failed: 6, including some UN document endpoints, one MONUSCO page, and the underlying Actualité.cd page for E042. E042 was therefore retained as reused from the supplied ledger, not counted as newly verified evidence.
- Distinct organizations among accepted/reused evidence: United Nations/MONUSCO/OHCHR, Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, U.S. Department of State, Committee to Protect Journalists, DRC Presidency, Actualité.cd, and Government of Rwanda.
- Source types: UN monitoring/Secretary-General reports, NGO investigations and annual reviews, government country report, official presidential record, local media, press-freedom incident investigation, and adverse foreign-government statement.

Lens coverage:

- 3B.1: State killings, torture, arbitrary detention, and conflict-related deaths covered.
- 3B.2: FARDC, police, intelligence, and militia abuse plus some prosecutions covered.
- 3B.3: No verified personal incitement by Tshisekedi found. His direct anti-discrimination intervention is covered; government-level adverse allegations remain contextual.
- 3B.4: Convictions, appellate correction, training, proposed victim-protection legislation, and major impunity limitations covered.
- 3B.5: State-of-siege extensions, military jurisdiction over civilians, and protest restrictions covered.
- 3B.6: Conflict exposure, state abuses, worsening civilian fatalities, and attribution constraints covered.
- 3B.7: Sexual violence, child casualties/abductions, displacement, ethnic hate speech, training, and proposed reparations covered.
- 3B.8: Peaceful protest, activist detention, journalist abuse, and one successful appeal covered.
- 3B.9: Protest responses, anti-UN unrest, conflict diplomacy, hate-speech response, and militarized emergency measures covered.
- 3B.10: Civilian deaths, displacement, armed-group predominance, worsening state-of-siege outcomes, and protection efforts covered.

Exact residual gaps:

- No reliable national denominator for torture, detention, protest repression, or victim remedies.
- No evidence establishing that Tshisekedi personally ordered individual killings, torture, journalist arrests, or protest violence.
- No independently verified 2022 evidence that Tshisekedi personally incited ethnic hatred; the adverse record concerns government officials collectively.
- Prosecution totals do not establish final appeals, sentence execution, victim compensation, command responsibility, or deterrence.
- Proposed protection and reparations laws do not demonstrate enactment or effective access.
- Conflict-area access restrictions and source overlap prevent clean nationwide trend or causal inference.
- The 2021-to-2022 security comparison cannot separate state-of-siege effects from renewed M23 and other armed-group activity.

A further general Chapter 3B wave is unlikely to add material value. A narrowly targeted archive wave could still improve only three residual issues: final dispositions of the 2022 security-force convictions, implementation status of victim/reparations legislation, and authenticated transcripts of senior officials accused of anti-Rwandophone incitement. Those are precision gaps rather than broad evidence-coverage gaps.
